sources.news_title: U.S. judge again blocks Trump’s makeover plan for D.C. golf course | Honolulu Star-Advertiser

U.S. judge again blocks Trump’s makeover plan for D.C. golf course
WASHINGTON >> A federal judge on Saturday ordered that a riverside public park in Washington must remain open for now, rather than being closed for renovations sought by President Donald Trump.
It is the latest setback for Trump’s plan to turn East Potomac Park into a championship-level course geared toward professional golfers. In a social media post later on Sunday, Trump denounced the judge’s decision.
In a 30-page decision, U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes temporarily blocked the federal government from moving forward with a plan that would have closed the area on Sunday.
Trump said last month the closure would last 15 months and would transform the park’s golf offerings into “one of the Best and Most Spectacular Golf Courses anywhere in the World.”
Reyes ruled that the Trump administration’s stated reasons for closing the park were “pretextual” and that the government violated at least two federal laws “to meet an arbitrary deadline.”
“The government proposes to close a historic park, daily enjoyed by Washingtonians of all stripes, indefinitely,” Reyes wrote.

Stay in touch with breaking news, as it happens, conveniently in your email inbox. It's FREE!
Although Reyes ordered that the park — near the Jefferson Memorial, 2 miles (3 km) south of the White House — remain open, the Trump administration does not have to maintain golf operations at the site, the judge wrote. But the government “cannot use the absence of golf operations as a reason to exclude the public,” she added.
Latest setback for Trump’s plans
The ruling by Reyes, who was appointed by Democratic President Joe Biden, is the latest instance of the federal judiciary pushing back against Trump’s sweeping efforts to redesign the nation’s capital through major construction projects.
In a post to his Truth Social network on Sunday, Trump said Reyes had delayed the park’s necessary refurbishment.
“Why would a judge want to delay taking a terrible and very unsafe golf course, one that is mocked all over DC (and far beyond!), instead of quickly turning it into a great and admired one?” he said.
Trump said the government would “immediately appeal on an expedited basis.” Temporary restraining orders, such as those issued by Reyes on Saturday, are generally not subject to appeal, however.
The ruling came in a lawsuit brought by the DC Preservation League, a historic preservation group that says Trump’s plan to redevelop the park violates various federal regulations and statutes. The group’s lawyers earlier won a ruling from Reyes that blocked the National Park Service, part of the Interior Department, from cutting down trees at the park or making other irreversible modifications without advance notice.
Democracy Forward, which is representing the preservation league and two local residents in the case, said in a statement it was grateful that Reyes stopped “another one of the president’s vanity projects.”
The group’s senior legal adviser, Catherine Carroll, said: “The administration’s inexplicable drive to destroy East Potomac Park would have taken away a treasured park that could never be replaced.”
The Interior and Justice Departments did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
The lawsuit has produced several heated confrontations between Reyes and Justice Department lawyers. The judge said last month that the government’s removal of hundreds of trees from the course and failure to tell the preservation group about the work “has cost the government all of its credibility” in the case.
Reyes has ordered an ethics investigation into whether government lawyers have repeatedly misled her about the timeline for the park’s closure.
The Justice Department has accused Reyes of overstepping her authority and inappropriately belittling government lawyers. It demanded her recusal from the case, a request she denied.
Trump, who owns golf courses globally, has focused on the East Potomac Park renovations as part of his larger ambition to leave an architectural legacy across Washington.
The park has three golf courses totaling 36 holes, a miniature golf course and a paved loop popular with cyclists and runners. The proposed redesign would turn the area into a single 18-hole championship course that Trump has said could hold world-class events, such as the US Open and the Ryder Cup, while remaining open to the public.

sources.news_title: Judge Blocks Trump East Potomac Golf Course Closure Plan
sources.text:
A federal judge has temporarily blocked the Trump administration from closing East Potomac Park, stalling a planned championship golf course as activist groups cheer the delay.
U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes ruled Saturday that East Potomac Park must stay open to the public for at least two more weeks, stopping a planned weekend shutdown tied to a major golf course renovation near Washington.
The Hill reported that the order bars the closure from moving ahead and keeps the historic park accessible except for routine, temporary safety shutdowns. The fight centers on President Trump’s push to replace the existing public links with an 18-hole championship-length course designed by architect Tom Fazio.
The ruling came after an hours-long Friday hearing. It expands an earlier court limit on tree cutting at the site and preserves the status quo while the case continues.
In a 30-page ruling, Reyes found that an indefinite closure would hurt regular park users and cut against the public interest in national parkland.
She wrote that the park “shall remain open and accessible to the public” except for “routine, temporary closures” needed to address imminent threats to public safety.
"The Government proposes to close a historic park, daily enjoyed by Washingtonians of all stripes, indefinitely. This closure would irreparably harm Plaintiffs, who use the Park regularly for recreational activities."
Reyes also said the government had not shown real harm from a short order that simply holds conditions in place pending further proceedings.
The New York Post reported the temporary restraining order runs through Nov. 28, 2026, and keeps the park and course open during normal hours while related litigation continues. Plaintiffs include the DC Preservation League and two local golfers. They argued redevelopment would change the course’s accessible character and drive up costs.
The same account said Trump had announced a Nov. 15 closure for renovation into what he described as a world championship public facility, even as a lawsuit filed earlier in the year remained pending. Reyes pointed to his public statements as evidence the plan was final and that a shutdown was imminent, points she said favored another short block.
Justice Department lawyers told the court the closure was about more than construction timing. A top lawyer for DOJ’s Energy and Natural Resources Division cited damaged seawall conditions, regular flooding, and the end of day-to-day control by the nonprofit that had run the courses.
National Links Trust was set to stop operating Sunday. The Trump administration terminated its lease last year. Reyes called the lack of an operator “self-inflicted,” but she did not order the government to take over active management of the park or the golf course.
"It does not order the Government to undertake any active management of either."
That leaves a practical gap. The course was headed toward a long renovation window. The order freezes the shutdown without forcing federal managers to run daily operations in the nonprofit’s place.
DOJ, for its part, stressed what the ruling does not stop. A department spokesperson said the court recognized that the National Park Service can still limit access when the public faces harm, and that planning work can continue.
"The Court has acknowledged that the National Park Service can limit access to its facilities where the public is at risk of harm. Nothing in the Court’s order precludes planning for the development of a world class golf course to continue."
The spokesperson added that the department will “always vociferously defend the Trump Administration’s agenda in court.”
Reyes pressed the government on urgency. The deteriorating seawall condition had been documented for more than a decade. That timeline undercut the claim that only an immediate weekend closure could handle safety risk.
At the same time, the administration had already moved hard on site prep. Hundreds of trees were cut in October. An earlier ruling then blocked further cutting and allowed safety-related work only with advance notice. Saturday’s order built on that restraint and applied it to the broader shutdown plan.
Just the News reported the course had been set to close Sunday for a year of renovations, and that Trump has long criticized the layout. He has called the site “Trash Island,” arguing the fairways sit too close together and the design itself drives golfers away.
That critique is the core of the administration’s project case: rebuild a weak public facility into a serious championship venue rather than leave a flawed course in place. Plaintiffs answer that the safety story is a pretext for a tournament-style redesign, including a layout critics say would stretch more than 8,000 yards from the back tees.
Outside court, left-aligned legal activists framed the pause as a win against the president personally. Catherine Carroll, senior legal advisor at Democracy Forward, cast the renovation as an attack on an irreplaceable park.
"We are grateful that once again, a court has intervened to prevent irreparable harm caused by the Trump-Vance administration’s pursuit of another one of the president’s vanity projects. The administration’s inexplicable drive to destroy East Potomac Park would have taken away a treasured park that could never be replaced, and we are honored to work with this coalition to secure this temporary relief."
The language is maximal. The order itself is not. It is a short pause. It does not kill the Fazio design. It does not ban planning. It does not convert every safety limit into a permanent veto. It holds the gates open for two weeks while lawyers keep fighting.
Hains Point also surfaced in the government’s discussion of sudden closure pressure. The operative public-access language in the ruling is tied to East Potomac Park, and the immediate effect is clear enough for park users: the weekend shutdown is off, and ordinary public access remains the baseline.
Several hard questions remain after Reyes’s order. If National Links Trust is gone and the court will not require active federal management, who runs the property day to day during the freeze? What seawall fixes count as “imminent” safety work with notice, and what counts as banned redevelopment?
The plaintiffs wanted a brake on irreversible change. The administration wanted to start converting a troubled public course into a higher-grade facility. For now, the brake is on, temporary, written, and narrow.
Two weeks is not a final judgment on the golf course. It is another chapter in a familiar pattern: executive action to rebuild public assets, met at the courthouse door by coalitions determined to slow the work.

Golf-crazy Trump to appeal ruling keeping Washington park open
A judge keeps East Potomac Park open for now, blocking plans to shut the public space for a golf course renovation.
WASHINGTON: US President Donald Trump criticised a judge's ruling that a park in the heart of Washington must remain open to the public, after his administration sought to close it for a golf course renovation.
An avid golfer who owns courses around the world, Trump aims to turn Washington's East Potomac Golf Links, a public course with affordable rates, into a facility capable of hosting major championship-caliber events.
"Why would a judge want to delay taking a terrible and very unsafe golf course, one that is mocked all over DC (and far beyond!), instead of quickly turning it into a great and admired one?" Trump wrote on Truth Social.
The US president added that his administration will appeal the "highly destructive and political decision of the judge."
The Trump administration has called for the Nov 15 closure of East Potomac Park, a 160-hectare expanse where the golf course is located, to begin construction.
But a lawsuit filed by an environmental group blocked the closure, with US District Judge Ana Reyes on Saturday granting a temporary restraining order that required the park remain open for now as the lawsuit works its way through the courts.
"The Government proposes to close a historic park, daily enjoyed by Washingtonians of all stripes, indefinitely," Reyes wrote in the 30-page ruling. "This closure would irreparably harm Plaintiffs, who use the Park regularly for recreational activities."
She had previously ruled against the early demolition work conducted for the project, including the cutting down of more than 500 trees along the course.
The golf course is one of several projects launched by Trump in a bid to put his personal stamp on the US capital, such as the White House ballroom and a massive triumphal arch, despite fierce local opposition and multiple legal challenges.

Trump blasts judge’s 2-week halt to his Washington golf project and says administration will appeal
sources.text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump on Sunday decried a “highly destructive and political decision” from a federal judge who ordered a two-week delay on renovations at a historic Washington public golf course that he has been trying to redevelop into a championship-level venue.
In a social media post, Trump said his administration will “immediately appeal, on an expedited basis” the temporary restraining order from U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes, which she issued just before East Potomac Golf Links was due to close Sunday for 15 months.
“It is in a terrible state of disrepair, as anybody can see by just looking at the pictures that are now circulating all over the Country, and in the Court,” said Trump, who spent much of the weekend posting photos on his social media site of the golf course. “They don’t call it Trash Island for no reason!”
Trump had announced work on the site along the Potomac River would begin that day despite the legal challenge initiated against the project in February by the DC Preservation League and two local golfers.
The plaintiffs argue that the president’s plan would change the character of the accessible golf course and make it unaffordable, something Trump has denied. They had sought the stop-work order, saying that closing the course and launching work on the project would “irreparably injure plaintiffs and the public interest.”
The president’s public announcements on social media last month outlining the date of the closure of East Potomac Park and linking it to the renovation of the golf course weighed heavily in the judge’s decision.
Reyes, in her ruling Saturday, noted that those posts presented a problem for the government, indicating that Trump’s redevelopment plan was final and that the National Park Service “will close the Park to implement it.”
Both points, she wrote, “favor granting Plaintiffs’ motion for another temporary restraining order.”
The order is in effect through Nov. 28. The park’s redevelopment is one of multiple projects in the nation’s capital that Trump has championed to remake the city. They include a large memorial arch, a White House ballroom and the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts, among others.
Reyes’ order was the latest in a series of rulings in lawsuits challenging Trump’s projects that were issued just hours before construction was expected to begin. A different judge recently ordered a 14-day delay on work for the arch, a decision that came shortly after a key planning commission stacked with Trump appointees approved plans for the project.
By SEUNG MIN KIM
Associated Press

The plaintiffs had asked Reyes to stop the closure, warning that shutting down the park and beginning construction would “irreparably injure plaintiffs and the public interest.”
Reyes agreed to temporarily halt the work after a lengthy hearing Friday, during which she repeatedly questioned the administration’s explanation for closing the property.
The Justice Department argued that the entire East Potomac Park was being closed because of safety concerns. The area includes three golf courses, a miniature golf course, bike paths and other recreational facilities. Government lawyers also pointed to the expiration of the lease held by the nonprofit National Links Trust, which currently operates the golf course.
But Reyes wasn’t buying the explanation so easily.
She noted that safety concerns had not been a central part of the administration’s argument for months. She also questioned whether the lease expiration was being used as a convenient justification for a closure that Trump had repeatedly demanded as part of his redevelopment plans.
In other words, the administration’s explanation wasn’t lining up with the president’s own public statements.
Trump, meanwhile, wasn’t exactly pleased with the judge’s intervention.

Trump insisted the project would become “something very special” and predicted that Reyes would eventually take pride in seeing the finished result.

sources.text:
Well, so much for that November 15 deadline.
The legal battle over President Donald Trump's plans to transform Washington, D.C.'s historic East Potomac Golf Course into a championship-level facility took another turn Saturday when U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes issued a 30-page temporary restraining order blocking the administration from closing the property as planned.
And this fight has become about considerably more than golf.
The administration had announced that East Potomac Park, including its golf course, would close Sunday to facilitate redevelopment. The National Park Service (NPS) subsequently cited safety concerns involving a deteriorating seawall and the impending departure of National Links Trust, which operates the course.
Reyes was not persuaded. (Par for the course.)
The Judge Tees Off
In her Saturday ruling, the judge concluded that those explanations were simply pretexts for carrying out Trump's directive to begin redeveloping the property. She pointed to the timing of the announcement, noting that seawall problems had been documented for years without prompting a park-wide closure. She also observed that more than 30,000 runners had participated in the Marine Corps Marathon around the park's perimeter just weeks earlier.
As for the golf course's impending lack of an operator, Reyes noted that NPS itself had arranged for National Links Trust's involvement to end November 15 — coincidentally, the very date Trump had selected for the closure.
But the ruling doesn't rest entirely on Reyes's skepticism of the government's explanations — there's also a rather significant regulatory wrinkle. Under NPS regulations, certain park closures that substantially alter public use or affect a park's scenic, natural, or cultural values require formal rulemaking.
Reyes concluded that shutting down most of East Potomac Park for an indefinite period — potentially years — triggers that requirement.
The agency hadn't completed the necessary process before Sunday's planned closure. Though the government submitted additional environmental and historic-preservation paperwork after Friday's hearing, that wasn't enough to persuade Reyes to allow the closure.
The judge also reiterated her earlier conclusion that the administration cannot implement portions of the broader golf-course redevelopment without first completing the environmental review required by federal law.
The government disputes that conclusion, maintaining that no final redevelopment decision has been made and that ordinary park-management decisions shouldn't automatically become subject to judicial intervention.
Alright, So Now What?
Under Reyes's order, the park and golf course must remain accessible to the public through November 28, unless the order is modified or terminated sooner.
The added hook (or slice)? The judge did not order NPS to keep the golf course operating for play or hire someone to run it. Officials may also temporarily restrict access to areas affected by active seawall repairs or imminent safety hazards, subject to reporting requirements. So the administration is left with some operational discretion, even as the court prevents the broader closure.
Meanwhile, the original preliminary injunction restricting further tree removal remains in effect, and the administration has already appealed that ruling to the D.C. Circuit.
The increasingly chippy proceedings have also spawned a separate dispute over Reyes' authority to investigate possible ethical violations by government attorneys, with the Justice Department objecting to her proposed appointment of a special master.
In other words, what began as a fight over trees and golf-course renovations has developed into a much larger confrontation over the boundaries of executive and judicial authority.
For the moment, Reyes has stopped the November 15 closure. Whether her interpretation of federal law — and the scope of her intervention — survives appellate scrutiny remains to be seen.
And something tells me the ultimate decision in this increasingly extraordinary legal battle may be made on the back nine.

By Gary Fields
A federal judge on Saturday ordered a two-week delay to any work at a historic Washington public golf course not far from the White House, blocking for now President Donald Trump’s push to redevelop the site along the Potomac River into a championship-level venue.
U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes issued the temporary restraining order before the East Potomac Golf Links was due to close Sunday for 15 months. Trump had announced work would begin that day despite the legal challenge initiated against the project in February by the DC Preservation League and two local golfers.
The plaintiffs argue that Trump’s plan would change the character of the accessible golf course and make it unaffordable, something the Republican president denies. They had sought the stop-work order, saying that closing the course and launching work on the project would “irreparably injure plaintiffs and the public interest.”
Trending
The president’s public announcements on social media last month outlining the date of the closure of East Potomac Park and linking it to the renovation of the golf course weighed heavily in the decision. Trump said on Oct. 26 that “We are closing the East Potomac Golf Course Site as scheduled on November 15th in order to renovate and rebuild for Competitive (with other such projects!), Safety, Modernization, and Aesthetic reasons.” He added that the goal was to renovate and rebuild ”a World Championship Public Facility.”
Reyes in her ruling Saturday noted that Trump’s posts presented a problem for the government. “They indicate that the Washington National Plan is final and that NPS will close the Park to implement it,” she wrote. “Both points favor granting Plaintiffs’ motion for another temporary restraining order.”
Reyes said her order “ENJOINS the government from closing East Potomac Park and the East Potomac Golf Course during the daily hours in which they were open as of November 14, 2026. It does not order the Government to undertake any active management of either. Further, for the avoidance of any doubt, the Government remains free, as it has since the onset of this litigation, to conduct repairs on any part of the Park and Course with any notice required by the existing Preliminary Injunction.”
The judge said the order is in effect “through November 28, 2026, or further order from the Court, whichever comes first.”
The Justice Department said in a statement Saturday that the judge acknowledged that the National Park Service can limit access to its facilities where the public is at risk of harm. “Nothing in the Court’s order precludes planning for the development of a world class golf course to continue,” it said. “The Department of Justice will always vociferously defend the Trump Administration’s agenda in court.”
Catherine Carroll, a senior legal adviser at Democracy Forward, which is representing the plaintiffs, praised the ruling. “We are grateful that once again, a court has intervened to prevent irreparable harm caused by the Trump-Vance administration’s pursuit of another one of the president’s vanity projects,” she said. “The administration’s inexplicable drive to destroy East Potomac Park would have taken away a treasured park that could never be replaced.”
The park’s redevelopment is one of multiple projects in the nation’s capital that Trump has championed to remake the city. They include a large memorial arch, a White House ballroom and the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts, among others.
Reyes had signaled throughout a five-hour court hearing Friday that she was likely to issue some stoppage for the park closure. The only issue was how expansive it might be. Justice Department lawyer Adam Gustafson argued that the entire East Potomac Park, which includes three golf courses, a miniature course, bike riding lanes and other recreational areas, was being closed because of safety factors. He also noted that the lease between the government and the current operator, National Links Trust, was ending Sunday.
Reyes pointed out that safety had not been part of the discussion over the closure for months and that ending the lease felt more like an action that provided a premise for the closure rather than an action that led to the closure of the course about 2 miles from the White House.
Even before the order, Trump lashed out in a social media post Saturday, contending that Reyes “doesn’t want us to quickly and inexpensively fix up the Course which is, also, very dangerous.” He said people who live in the Washington area would get a 50% discount on “any and all Rates charged” and that the redevelopment would “evolve into something very special, something which the Judge will be able to take great pride in seeing!”
Reyes’ order was the latest in a series of rulings in lawsuits challenging Trump’s projects that were issued just hours before construction was expected to begin. A different judge recently ordered a 14-day delay on work for the arch, a decision that came shortly after a key planning commission stacked with Trump appointees approved plans for the project.
Reyes, who was nominated to the court by Democratic President Joe Biden, had for months been reticent about approving the plaintiffs’ requests for work stoppages. The plaintiffs had argued the administration was moving ahead with work related to the project despite the pending lawsuit.
Her reluctance to issue orders ended in October, spurred in part by a tree-cutting spree by the administration over a holiday weekend with little notification to the judge or plaintiffs.
Officials and government lawyers said the tree work was part of a 2019 plan that recommended the cutting. In response, the judge confronted the administration over what she portrayed as deceitful actions over its intentions for the project.
Reyes has repeatedly expressed frustration over the minute planning details she has been asked to adjudicate, including over the trees being cut down at the 106-year-old park. WASHINGTON, Nov 14 (Reuters) – A federal judge on Saturday ordered that a riverside public park in Washington must remain open for now, rather than being closed for renovations sought by US President Donald Trump.
It is the latest setback for Trump’s plan to turn East Potomac Park into a championship-level course geared toward professional golfers.
In a 30-page decision, US District Judge Ana Reyes temporarily blocked the federal government from moving forward with a plan that would have closed the area on Sunday. Trump said in an October 18 social media post that the closure would last 15 months and would transform the park’s golf offerings into “one of the Best and Most Spectacular Golf Courses anywhere in the World.”
Reyes ruled that the Trump administration’s stated reasons for closing the park were “pretextual” and that the government violated at least two federal laws “to meet an arbitrary deadline.”
“The government proposes to close a historic park, daily enjoyed by Washingtonians of all stripes, indefinitely,” Reyes wrote.
Although Reyes ordered that the park – near the Jefferson Memorial, 2 miles (3 km) south of the White House – remain open, the Trump administration does not have to maintain golf operations at the site, the judge wrote. But the government “cannot use the absence of golf operations as a reason to exclude the public,” she added.
The ruling by Reyes, who was appointed by Democratic President Joe Biden and whom Trump has called a “lunatic,” is the latest instance of the federal judiciary pushing back against Trump’s sweeping efforts to redesign the nation’s capital through major construction projects.
The ruling came in a lawsuit brought by the DC Preservation League, a historic preservation group that says Trump’s plan to redevelop the park violates various federal regulations and statutes. The group’s lawyers earlier won a ruling from Reyes that blocked the National Park Service, part of the Interior Department, from cutting down trees at the park or making other irreversible modifications without advance notice.
Democracy Forward, which is representing the preservation league and two local residents in the case, said in a statement it was grateful that Reyes stopped “another one of the president’s vanity projects.”
The group’s senior legal adviser, Catherine Carroll, said: “The administration’s inexplicable drive to destroy East Potomac Park would have taken away a treasured park that could never be replaced.”
The Interior Department, Justice Department and the White House did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
The lawsuit has produced several heated confrontations between Reyes and Justice Department lawyers. The judge said last month that the government’s removal of hundreds of trees from the course and failure to tell the preservation group about the work “has cost the government all of its credibility” in the case.
Reyes has ordered an ethics investigation into whether government lawyers have repeatedly misled her about the timeline for the park’s closure.
The Justice Department has accused Reyes of overstepping her authority and inappropriately belittling government lawyers. It demanded her recusal from the case, a request she denied.
Trump, who owns golf courses globally, has focused on the East Potomac Park renovations as part of his larger ambition to leave an architectural legacy across Washington.
The park has three golf courses totaling 36 holes, a miniature golf course and a paved loop popular with cyclists and runners. The proposed redesign would turn the area into a single 18-hole championship course that Trump has said could hold world-class events, such as the US Open and the Ryder Cup, while remaining open to the public.

Judge temporarily blocks Trump from moving ahead on Washington public golf course redevelopment
A federal judge on Saturday ordered a two-week delay to any work at a historic Washington public golf course not far from the White House, blocking for now President Donald Trump's push to redevelop the site along the Potomac River into a championship-level venue.
U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes issued the temporary restraining order before the East Potomac Golf Links was due to close Sunday for 15 months. Trump had announced work would begin that day despite the legal challenge initiated against the project in February by the DC Preservation League and two local golfers.
Video above: Trump was 'kidding' about Dana White press secretary job offer
The plaintiffs argue that Trump's plan would change the character of the accessible golf course and make it unaffordable, something the Republican president denies. They had sought the stop-work order, saying that closing the course and launching work on the project would “irreparably injure plaintiffs and the public interest."
The president's public announcements on social media last month outlining the date of the closure of East Potomac Park and linking it to the renovation of the golf course weighed heavily in the decision. Trump said on Oct. 26 that “We are closing the East Potomac Golf Course Site as scheduled on November 15th in order to renovate and rebuild for Competitive (with other such projects!), Safety, Modernization, and Aesthetic reasons.” He added that the goal was to renovate and rebuild ”a World Championship Public Facility."
Reyes in her ruling Saturday noted that Trump's posts presented a problem for the government. “They indicate that the Washington National Plan is final and that NPS will close the Park to implement it,” she wrote. “Both points favor granting Plaintiffs’ motion for another temporary restraining order.”
Reyes said her order “ENJOINS the government from closing East Potomac Park and the East Potomac Golf Course during the daily hours in which they were open as of November 14, 2026. It does not order the Government to undertake any active management of either. Further, for the avoidance of any doubt, the Government remains free, as it has since the onset of this litigation, to conduct repairs on any part of the Park and Course with any notice required by the existing Preliminary Injunction.”
The judge said the order is in effect “through November 28, 2026, or further order from the Court, whichever comes first.”
The Justice Department said in a statement Saturday that the judge acknowledged that the National Park Service can limit access to its facilities where the public is at risk of harm. “Nothing in the Court’s order precludes planning for the development of a world class golf course to continue,” it said. "The Department of Justice will always vociferously defend the Trump Administration’s agenda in court.”
Catherine Carroll, a senior legal adviser at Democracy Forward, which is representing the plaintiffs, praised the ruling. “We are grateful that once again, a court has intervened to prevent irreparable harm caused by the Trump-Vance administration’s pursuit of another one of the president’s vanity projects,” she said. “The administration’s inexplicable drive to destroy East Potomac Park would have taken away a treasured park that could never be replaced."
The park’s redevelopment is one of multiple projects in the nation's capital that Trump has championed to remake the city. They include a large memorial arch, a White House ballroom and the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts, among others.
Reyes had signaled throughout a five-hour court hearing Friday that she was likely to issue some stoppage for the park closure. The only issue was how expansive it might be. Justice Department lawyer Adam Gustafson argued that the entire East Potomac Park, which includes three golf courses, a miniature course, bike riding lanes and other recreational areas, was being closed because of safety factors. He also noted that the lease between the government and the current operator, National Links Trust, was ending Sunday.
Reyes pointed out that safety had not been part of the discussion over the closure for months and that ending the lease felt more like an action that provided a premise for the closure rather than an action that led to the closure of the course about 2 miles from the White House.
Video below: President Donald Trump Veterans Day event
Even before the order, Trump lashed out in a social media post Saturday, contending that Reyes “doesn’t want us to quickly and inexpensively fix up the Course which is, also, very dangerous.” He said people who live in the Washington area would get a 50% discount on “any and all Rates charged” and that the redevelopment would “evolve into something very special, something which the Judge will be able to take great pride in seeing!”
Reyes’ order was the latest in a series of rulings in lawsuits challenging Trump’s projects that were issued just hours before construction was expected to begin. A different judge recently ordered a 14-day delay on work for the arch, a decision that came shortly after a key planning commission stacked with Trump appointees approved plans for the project.
Reyes, who was nominated to the court by Democratic President Joe Biden, had for months been reticent about approving the plaintiffs’ requests for work stoppages. The plaintiffs had argued the administration was moving ahead with work related to the project despite the pending lawsuit.
Her reluctance to issue orders ended in October, spurred in part by a tree-cutting spree by the administration over a holiday weekend with little notification to the judge or plaintiffs.
Officials and government lawyers said the tree work was part of a 2019 plan that recommended the cutting. In response, the judge confronted the administration over what she portrayed as deceitful actions over its intentions for the project.
Reyes has repeatedly expressed frustration over the minute planning details she has been asked to adjudicate, including over the trees being cut down at the 106-year-old park. The Justice Department filed a request that Reyes be removed from the case because of what it called her “egregious behavior” and questioned her impartiality. Reyes has not recused herself.
The restraining order was one of two issues Reyes took up during Friday's hearing.
She announced plans last week to name Jessie Liu, a former U.S. attorney for the District of Columbia, to examine whether officials with the Interior Department and the National Park Service and attorneys with the Justice Department had violated ethics or misled her during the course of the case.
Associated Press writer Eric Tucker contributed to this report.

sources.text:
A Biden-appointed federal judge stepped in late Saturday and temporarily blocked the government from closing East Potomac Golf Course—just hours before President Trump’s roughly 15-month overhaul was scheduled to begin.
U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes did not permanently kill the project. Her temporary restraining order keeps East Potomac Park and the golf course open during their existing daily hours through November 28, or until the court orders otherwise, while the legal fight moves forward.
The Trump administration’s vision is no minor touch-up. Interior Secretary Doug Burgum unveiled a Fazio Design plan in May that he said would give the National Capital Region a championship-quality public course with steeply discounted rates for local residents.
The breaking order landed late Saturday, with the planned Sunday closure only hours away:
Judge temporarily blocks Trump from moving ahead on Washington public golf course redevelopment https://t.co/MK83o1fjaf
— The Associated Press (@AP) November 15, 2026
But the planned November 15 closure ran straight into the lawsuit brought by the D.C. Preservation League and two golfers.
In Saturday’s 30-page temporary restraining order, Reyes said the plaintiffs were likely to succeed on claims that the National Park Service violated the National Environmental Policy Act and the Administrative Procedure Act. Those are preliminary findings at the emergency-relief stage, not a final judgment on the merits.
The judge found that shutting the park and course for the renovation would change the status quo while the litigation is still pending. She also treated Trump’s prior public announcement of a final plan and a November 15 closing date as evidence that the government intended to implement the redesign.
The relief is tightly defined. The government cannot close the park or course during the hours they were open on November 14, but the order does not force it to run golf operations or sign a new concession contract.
Repairs remain allowed under the court’s earlier notice rules, and officials may temporarily restrict the immediate area around a genuine safety hazard. The order requires notice within 24 hours and a sworn declaration from a senior Park Service employee if an imminent danger forces such a restriction.
The Associated Press reported that the public course had been set to close Sunday for about 15 months and that its operator, National Links Trust, had already begun preparing for the shutdown. The park includes more than golf: the disputed closure also covered public roads and recreational areas used by cyclists, runners and other visitors.
The Justice Department said planning for a world-class course may continue and emphasized that the judge left room to limit access where the public faces actual danger. The plaintiffs, meanwhile, argued that closing the park before the court could decide the case would cause irreparable harm.
That distinction matters. Saturday’s order preserves public access for two weeks; it does not award either side a final victory over the redesign, resolve the environmental claims, or establish what the finished course may cost golfers.
The final language even tells the parties that the court will be available Sunday for emergency clarification. That unusual detail arrived after months of disputes over notice and compliance:
ALERT: Judge Ana Reyes extends HALT of Trump takeover of East Potomac golf course
And after multiple incidents of alleged non-compliance with her court orders, Reyes adds a little “call if you need clarification” note in her order pic.twitter.com/5iYseolygU
— Scott MacFarlane (@MacFarlaneNews) November 15, 2026
Reyes had already issued an October 26 preliminary injunction restricting further tree removal and requiring ten business days’ advance notice before the government made additional irreparable changes to the site.
The group opposing the overhaul quickly celebrated the access ruling while acknowledging an important limit: the judge did not order the government to keep operating the golf course itself.
NEWS: East Potomac Park is not closing tomorrow.
Reyes has put in place a TRO to prevent entire closure of the park. She has not mandated that they continue operating the course.
129 years and counting. This park will remain open to all of us.
— Save East Po (@SaveEastPo) November 15, 2026
Trump answered with a very different picture of what he wants to build.
In his direct Saturday statement, the president argued that the existing layout is unsafe because fairways run too close together, called for a cleaner and more beautiful course, and said the redesign could produce a championship venue worthy of a major tournament. He also promoted a 50% rate reduction for D.C.-area residents.
Trump sharply criticized Reyes and branded the current property “Trash Island,” saying Interior should be allowed to turn what he considers one of the country’s worst courses into its best. Those are the president’s judgments and political response to the order.
The headline’s political lineage is not in dispute. The Federal Judicial Center records that President Joe Biden first nominated Reyes to the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia in May 2022, but the Senate did not vote before that nomination expired.
Biden nominated her again on January 3, 2023. The Senate confirmed her on February 15, and she received her commission six days later after more than two decades in private practice in Washington.
That biography verifies who put Reyes on the bench; it does not decide whether her emergency legal findings will survive the next stage of this case.
For now, the public keeps access to East Potomac during its normal hours, and the government may continue permitted repairs and planning. The Biden judge has postponed the scheduled closure while she weighs the challenge, but the final fate of Trump’s overhaul remains unresolved.

U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes issued the temporary restraining order before the East Potomac Golf Links was due to close Sunday for 15 months. Trump had announced work would begin that day despite the legal challenge initiated against the project in February by the DC Preservation League and two local golfers.
The plaintiffs argue that Trump’s plan would change the character of the accessible golf course and make it unaffordable, something the Republican president denies. They had sought the stop-work order, saying that closing the course and launching work on the project would “irreparably injure plaintiffs and the public interest.”
The president’s public announcements on social media last month outlining the date of the closure of East Potomac Park and linking it to the renovation of the golf course weighed heavily in the decision. Trump said on Oct. 26 that “We are closing the East Potomac Golf Course Site as scheduled on November 15th in order to renovate and rebuild for Competitive (with other such projects!), Safety, Modernization, and Aesthetic reasons.” He added that the goal was to renovate and rebuild ”a World Championship Public Facility.”
Reyes in her ruling Saturday noted that Trump’s posts presented a problem for the government. “They indicate that the Washington National Plan is final and that NPS will close the Park to implement it,” she wrote. “Both points favor granting Plaintiffs’ motion for another temporary restraining order.”
Reyes said her order “ENJOINS the government from closing East Potomac Park and the East Potomac Golf Course during the daily hours in which they were open as of November 14, 2026. It does not order the Government to undertake any active management of either. Further, for the avoidance of any doubt, the Government remains free, as it has since the onset of this litigation, to conduct repairs on any part of the Park and Course with any notice required by the existing Preliminary Injunction.”
The judge said the order is in effect “through November 28, 2026, or further order from the Court, whichever comes first.”
The Justice Department said in a statement Saturday that the judge acknowledged that the National Park Service can limit access to its facilities where the public is at risk of harm. “Nothing in the Court’s order precludes planning for the development of a world class golf course to continue,” it said. “The Department of Justice will always vociferously defend the Trump Administration’s agenda in court.”
Catherine Carroll, a senior legal adviser at Democracy Forward, which is representing the plaintiffs, praised the ruling. “We are grateful that once again, a court has intervened to prevent irreparable harm caused by the Trump-Vance administration’s pursuit of another one of the president’s vanity projects,” she said. “The administration’s inexplicable drive to destroy East Potomac Park would have taken away a treasured park that could never be replaced.”
The park’s redevelopment is one of multiple projects in the nation’s capital that Trump has championed to remake the city. They include a large memorial arch, a White House ballroom and the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts, among others.
Reyes had signaled throughout a five-hour court hearing Friday that she was likely to issue some stoppage for the park closure. The only issue was how expansive it might be. Justice Department lawyer Adam Gustafson argued that the entire East Potomac Park, which includes three golf courses, a miniature course, bike riding lanes and other recreational areas, was being closed because of safety factors. He also noted that the lease between the government and the current operator, National Links Trust, was ending Sunday.
Reyes pointed out that safety had not been part of the discussion over the closure for months and that ending the lease felt more like an action that provided a premise for the closure rather than an action that led to the closure of the course about 2 miles from the White House.

The restraining order was one of two issues Reyes took up during Friday’s hearing.
She announced plans last week to name Jessie Liu, a former U.S. attorney for the District of Columbia, to examine whether officials with the Interior Department and the National Park Service and attorneys with the Justice Department had violated ethics or misled her during the course of the case.

Reyes has for months been overseeing a challenge to the president's plans for East Potomac Golf Links, a public course in Washington that opened in the 1920s. The dispute escalated last month when the National Park Service notified the judge that it would be removing trees on the course and went on to cut down more than 500 trees in the span of a weekend.
Reyes then issued an order blocking the Trump administration from felling any additional trees, and required the Justice Department to provide her with notice of any future actions the National Park Service planned to take at the golf course.
Mr. Trump, meanwhile, announced last month that East Potomac would close Nov. 15 to allow work on the new design by Fazio to begin, with the renovated "world-class, championship course" expected to open in roughly 15 months.

The Trump administration argued that the entirety of the park had to be closed because of a deteriorating sea wall, safety risks at the golf course, and because the organization that was overseeing the course, the National Links Trust, would cease operating it as of Nov. 15.

sources.news_title: Judge blocks Trump from moving ahead on East Potomac Golf Links redevelopment
sources.text:
A federal judge on Saturday ordered a temporary stop to any work at a historic Washington, D.C., public golf course not far from the White House, blocking for now President Donald Trump's push to redevelop the site along the Potomac River into a championship-level venue.
U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes issued the temporary restraining order before East Potomac Golf Links was due to close Sunday for 15 months. Trump had announced work would begin that day despite the legal challenge initiated against the project in February by the DC Preservation League and two local golfers.
Stream NBC4 newscasts for free right here, right now.
The plaintiffs argue that Trump's plan would change the character of the accessible golf course and make it unaffordable, something the Republican president denies. They had sought the stop-work order, saying that closing the course and launching work on the project would “irreparably injure plaintiffs and the public interest."
The park’s redevelopment is one of multiple projects in the nation's capital that Trump has championed to remake the city. They include a large memorial arch, a White House ballroom and the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts, among others.
Reyes had signaled throughout a five-hour court hearing Friday that she was likely to issue some stoppage for the park closure. The only issue was how expansive it might be. Justice Department lawyer Adam Gustafson argued that the entire East Potomac Park, which includes three golf courses, a miniature course, bike riding lanes and other recreational areas, was being closed because of safety factors. He also noted that the lease between the government and the current operator, National Links Trust, was ending Sunday.
Reyes pointed out that safety had not been part of the discussion over the closure for months and that ending the lease felt more like an action that provided a premise for the closure rather than an action that led to the closure of the course about 2 miles from the White House.
She also rejected Gustafson's argument that the closure was separate from Trump's repeated pronouncements that he wanted the course to be closed and renovated into a world-class venue and had called repeatedly for the park's closure by the deadline as part of what is known as the Washington National plan.
Even before the order, Trump lashed out in a social media post Saturday, contending that Reyes “doesn’t want us to quickly and inexpensively fix up the Course which is, also, very dangerous.” He said people who live in the Washington area would get a 50% discount on “any and all Rates charged” and that the redevelopment would “evolve into something very special, something which the Judge will be able to take great pride in seeing!”
Reyes’ order was the latest in a series of rulings in lawsuits challenging Trump’s projects that were issued just hours before construction was expected to begin. A different judge recently ordered a 14-day delay on work for the arch, a decision that came shortly after a key planning commission stacked with Trump appointees approved plans for the project.
Reyes, who was nominated to the court by Democratic President Joe Biden, had for months been reticent about approving the plaintiffs’ requests for work stoppages. The plaintiffs had argued the administration was moving ahead with work related to the project despite the pending lawsuit.
Her reluctance to issue orders ended in October, spurred in part by a tree-cutting spree by the administration over a holiday weekend with little notification to the judge or plaintiffs.
Officials and government lawyers said the tree work was part of a 2019 plan that recommended the cutting. In response, the judge confronted the administration over what she portrayed as deceitful actions over its intentions for the project.
Reyes has repeatedly expressed frustration over the minute planning details she has been asked to adjudicate, including over the trees being cut down at the 106-year-old park. The Justice Department filed a request that Reyes be removed from the case because of what it called her “egregious behavior” and questioned her impartiality. Reyes has not recused herself.
The restraining order was one of two issues Reyes took up during Friday's hearing.
She announced plans last week to name Jessie Liu, a former U.S. attorney for the District of Columbia, to examine whether officials with the Interior Department and the National Park Service and attorneys with the Justice Department had violated ethics or misled her during the course of the case. Gustafson asked her to reconsider and give the Justice Department the opportunity to show an outside investigator was unnecessary.
“It's quite a cloud on the people it affects,” he said.
Reyes said she understood.
“To be frank with you I don’t want to do this,” she said, but she had an ethical obligation to at least look because "I think there is enough smoke that someone needs to consider whether there’s been fire.”

sources.news_title: US judge again blocks Trump’s makeover plan for DC golf course
sources.text:
By Jan Wolfe and David Thomas
WASHINGTON, Nov 14 (Reuters) – A federal judge on Saturday ordered that a riverside public park in Washington must remain open for now, rather than being closed for renovations sought by US President Donald Trump.
It is the latest setback for Trump’s plan to turn East Potomac Park into a championship-level course geared toward professional golfers. In a social media post later on Sunday, Trump denounced the judge’s decision.
In a 30-page decision, US District Judge Ana Reyes temporarily blocked the federal government from moving forward with a plan that would have closed the area on Sunday.
Trump said last month the closure would last 15 months and would transform the park’s golf offerings into “one of the Best and Most Spectacular Golf Courses anywhere in the World.”
Reyes ruled that the Trump administration’s stated reasons for closing the park were “pretextual” and that the government violated at least two federal laws “to meet an arbitrary deadline.”
“The government proposes to close a historic park, daily enjoyed by Washingtonians of all stripes, indefinitely,” Reyes wrote.
Although Reyes ordered that the park — near the Jefferson Memorial, 2 miles (3 km) south of the White House — remain open, the Trump administration does not have to maintain golf operations at the site, the judge wrote. But the government “cannot use the absence of golf operations as a reason to exclude the public,” she added.
LATEST SETBACK FOR TRUMP’S PLANS
The ruling by Reyes, who was appointed by Democratic President Joe Biden, is the latest instance of the federal judiciary pushing back against Trump’s sweeping efforts to redesign the nation’s capital through major construction projects.
In a post to his Truth Social network on Sunday, Trump said Reyes had delayed the park’s necessary refurbishment.
“Why would a judge want to delay taking a terrible and very unsafe golf course, one that is mocked all over DC (and far beyond!), instead of quickly turning it into a great and admired one?” he said.
Trump said the government would “immediately appeal on an expedited basis.” Temporary restraining orders, such as those issued by Reyes on Saturday, are generally not subject to appeal, however.
The ruling came in a lawsuit brought by the DC Preservation League, a historic preservation group that says Trump’s plan to redevelop the park violates various federal regulations and statutes. The group’s lawyers earlier won a ruling from Reyes that blocked the National Park Service, part of the Interior Department, from cutting down trees at the park or making other irreversible modifications without advance notice.
Democracy Forward, which is representing the preservation league and two local residents in the case, said in a statement it was grateful that Reyes stopped “another one of the president’s vanity projects.”
The group’s senior legal adviser, Catherine Carroll, said: “The administration’s inexplicable drive to destroy East Potomac Park would have taken away a treasured park that could never be replaced.”
The Interior and Justice Departments did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
The lawsuit has produced several heated confrontations between Reyes and Justice Department lawyers. The judge said last month that the government’s removal of hundreds of trees from the course and failure to tell the preservation group about the work “has cost the government all of its credibility” in the case.
Reyes has ordered an ethics investigation into whether government lawyers have repeatedly misled her about the timeline for the park’s closure.
The Justice Department has accused Reyes of overstepping her authority and inappropriately belittling government lawyers. It demanded her recusal from the case, a request she denied.
Trump, who owns golf courses globally, has focused on the East Potomac Park renovations as part of his larger ambition to leave an architectural legacy across Washington.
The park has three golf courses totaling 36 holes, a miniature golf course and a paved loop popular with cyclists and runners. The proposed redesign would turn the area into a single 18-hole championship course that Trump has said could hold world-class events, such as the US Open and the Ryder Cup, while remaining open to the public.
(Reporting by Jan Wolfe and David Thomas; Additional writing by David Thomas and Douglas Gillison; Editing by Tomasz Janowski, Sergio Non, William Mallard and Christina Fincher)
